(1) a planar graph with n vertices can be made sparse by removing a set of O(n1/3) edges that partition the graph into subgraphs with O(n1/4) vertices, and (2) the sparsification can be maintained in O(n1+ε) total time per insertion and deletion, and can be queried in O(1) time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing data structures for maintaining planar graphs that are sparse, and yet that preserve the connectivity of the graph.
the design and analysis of data structures and algorithms for the dynamic maintenance of planar graphs subject to insertions and deletions of edges that preserve the planarity of the graph.
the design of dynamic data structures for planar graphs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the separator-based sparsification method is the best method for maintaining connectivity in planar graphs, in particular in dynamic planar graphs.
the separator based sparsification technique is a powerful and versatile tool for dynamic algorithms in planar graphs.
the problem of maintaining 3-vertex connectivity in a dynamic planar graphs subject to insertions that maintain planarity can be solved in O(n1.5) amortized time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we can maintain a graph subject to edge deletions or insertions that preserve planar embeddings in O(n1.5) amortized time and maintain information on the 2- or 3-vertex and 3- or 4-edge-connectivities in O(n1+epsilon) amortized time for any fixed constant epsilon > 0.

, given any planar graph with n vertices, m edges, k components, and t triconnected components, one can maintain a data structure in O(m + n log n) time that answers queries about the connectivity properties of the graph in O(log n + k + t) time, where the queries are about 2- or 3-vertex connectivity or about 3- or 4-edge connectivity.
we have developed a new technique for maintaining connectivity properties of dynamic graphs that is based on sparsification and separators.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for many problems, we can maintain information about a graph in a way that allows us to handle insertions and deletions that do not preserve a particular embedding of the input graph.
, in planar graphs, it is sometimes possible to use separators to obtain algorithms with better running times than the standard approach of maintaining an Euler tour tree.
the planarity of the graph allows us to maintain connectivity information in a way that would be impossible in general graphs.
